title: Testes & Epididymis Anatomy
descriptor: Scrotum, Sperm Production, Epididymis & Deferent Duct, Torsion & Testicular Cancer
intro: The testes, also called the testicles, are a pair of egg-shaped glands that lie in the scrotum, the sac of loose skin below the penis. They make sperm and the hormone testosterone. Sperm pass from each testis into the epididymis, a coiled tube in which they mature, and then along the deferent duct, which joins the duct of the seminal vesicle near the prostate to form the ejaculatory duct. The seminal vesicles lie behind the bladder and add fluid to the semen.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: A pair of egg-shaped glands inside the scrotum, each a few centimetres long

keyFacts.label: Coverings
keyFacts.value: Outer tunica vaginalis, then the tough tunica albuginea, which folds inwards to divide the testis into lobules

keyFacts.label: Working tissue
keyFacts.value: Seminiferous tubules make sperm; Leydig cells between the tubules make testosterone

keyFacts.label: Sperm pathway
keyFacts.value: Epididymis (head, body and tail), then the deferent duct, which joins the seminal vesicle duct to form the ejaculatory duct

keyFacts.label: Temperature
keyFacts.value: Kept a few degrees below core body temperature, helped by the dartos and cremaster muscles

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Testicular arteries from the abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries; veins form the pampiniform plexus

keyFacts.label: Investigation
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound scan of the testicles and blood tests

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: Each testis lies in its own compartment of the scrotum, separated from the other testis by the scrotal septum. The dartos muscle forms the muscle layer beneath the scrotal skin and continues inwards to form that septum. Each testis is covered on the outside by the tunica vaginalis, and beneath this lies the tough, white tunica albuginea. A spermatic cord supports each testis, and the deferent duct runs through the cord on its way out of the scrotum. The two cremaster muscles descend from the internal oblique muscle of the abdominal wall.

sections.heading: Structure of the testis
sections.body:
The tunica albuginea also folds inwards to form septa that divide the testis into hundreds of lobules, and the septa converge on the mediastinum testis, which gives the organ structural support. The seminiferous tubules form the bulk of each testis, and sperm are made within them. The tubules end in straight tubules, the tubuli recti, which pass into the mediastinum and join a network of channels called the rete testis, and efferent ductules then connect the rete testis to the epididymis.

Leydig cells, which lie between the tubules, make testosterone. Sertoli cells help control the survival of the developing germ cells, and tight junctions between them form the blood-testis barrier. This barrier keeps bloodborne substances away from the germ cells and stops surface antigens on developing germ cells from escaping into the bloodstream and provoking an autoimmune response.

sections.heading: Epididymis, deferent duct and seminal vesicle
sections.body:
The epididymis is a coiled tube with a head, a body and a tail. Sperm continue to mature as they pass through it and are stored in the tail until ejaculation. The deferent duct is also known as the vas deferens or ductus deferens. It continues from the tail of the epididymis, and during ejaculation contraction of smooth muscle pushes sperm from the tail into the duct.

The deferent duct passes from the scrotum through the inguinal canal into the pelvis and then runs behind the prostate, and its far end widens into the ampulla near the back of the bladder. Each seminal vesicle lies behind the bladder and the prostate and above the rectum, beside the ampulla of the deferent duct, and the two join to form the ejaculatory duct, which drains into the prostatic urethra.

sections.heading: Blood supply, nerves and lymph
sections.body: The testicular arteries arise from the front and side of the abdominal aorta, just below the origin of the renal arteries, with additional supply from the artery of the vas deferens and the cremasteric artery. Venous blood leaves through the pampiniform plexus, a network of veins that lies in front of the deferent duct. The testes receive both sympathetic and parasympathetic nerve fibres. Lymph from the testes follows the same path as the testicular arteries and drains to the preaortic lymph nodes. The arteries to the seminal vesicles come from the middle and inferior vesical and middle rectal vessels.

sections.heading: Function: sperm, testosterone and temperature
sections.body:
The testes make sperm and androgens such as testosterone, and luteinising hormone binds to receptors on the Leydig cells and increases their production of testosterone.

Sperm production proceeds more efficiently when the testes are kept a few degrees below core body temperature. In cold weather the dartos and cremaster muscles contract to lift the testes towards the body and reduce the surface area of the scrotum, which retains heat; when the temperature rises the scrotum relaxes, which increases its surface area and promotes heat loss.

During ejaculation sperm travel through the deferent duct and mix with fluid from the accessory glands, and the seminal vesicles contribute the bulk of the volume of semen.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance: torsion and infection
sections.body: In testicular torsion the spermatic cord twists, which cuts off the blood supply to the testicle and can cause lasting damage. The most common sign of torsion is sudden, severe pain in one testicle, and NHS advice is to go straight to A&E or call 999. Epididymo-orchitis is inflammation of the epididymis and the testicle that can be caused by infection. The NHS says that epididymitis is usually triggered by a sexually transmitted infection or a urine infection, with less common triggers including mumps, tuberculosis and a groin injury. It causes a tender, warm, swollen scrotum, and some people also have difficulty passing urine or a discharge from the penis.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance: swellings and undescended testes
sections.body:
Most testicular lumps and swellings are not cancer. The commonest causes are a hydrocele, a cyst in the epididymis and varicose veins above the testicle, called a varicocele, and these are all benign and need treatment only if they cause significant symptoms. A hydrocele is fluid that collects between the layers of the tunica vaginalis, and a varicocele is an abnormal widening of the pampiniform plexus that usually occurs on the left.

An undescended testicle has not moved into the scrotum as it usually does, and the condition is common in young children. Often the testicle moves into place on its own, but sometimes surgery is needed, and doctors usually find the problem at the newborn examination. Left untreated, an undescended testis carries risks of reduced fertility, testicular torsion and a higher risk of testicular cancer.

sections.heading: Testicular cancer and how it is investigated
sections.body: Testicular cancer is a disease in which malignant cells form in the tissue of one or both testicles. The NHS lists a lump or swelling in a testicle, a testicle getting bigger, an ache or pain in the testicle or scrotum, and a heavy, firm or hard scrotum as the main symptoms. These symptoms can have other causes, but the NHS advises seeing a GP about any of them. A scrotal ultrasound scan will usually distinguish between benign and cancerous swellings. When testicular cancer is suspected, the NHS lists blood tests and an ultrasound scan of the testicles among the tests used, after which a specialist explains the results and the next steps.
